html:
A debate held at the Han dynasty court in 81 BCE over state control of the economy. Its record, edited a few decades later by the scholar Huan Kuan, is one of the earliest long arguments about the state and the market.

The emperor Emperor Wu had paid for wars against the Xiongnu by making salt and iron state monopolies, fixing prices and taxing merchants. After his death, the regent Huo Guang called scholars from the provinces to court to discuss the policies. On one side stood the chancellor Sang Hongyang and his officials, who said the monopolies kept the state strong and the borders safe. On the other stood Confucian scholars, who said the state should not compete with the people for profit, and that good government rests on virtue, not revenue.

The wine monopoly was dropped, but salt and iron stayed. The text has been quoted in Chinese debates over state enterprise ever since.
sum: A debate held at the Han dynasty court in 81 BCE over state control of the economy. Its record, edited a few decades later by the scholar Huan Kuan, is one of the earliest long arguments about the state and the market.
